name: Howard University
kind: Private HBCU · Federally chartered research university
affiliation: Federally chartered (Congress, 1867); founded by members of the First Congregational Society of Washington; named for Freedmen's Bureau commissioner Gen. Oliver O. Howard
description: Chartered by Congress on March 2, 1867, Howard grew from a proposed seminary for Black clergy into a comprehensive university with liberal arts, medicine, law, business, communications and engineering. It is the only HBCU with an R1 research classification and receives an annual congressional appropriation. Its law school trained the NAACP legal team that won Brown v. Board, and its alumni network is the largest in this map — spanning Wall Street, broadcasting, hospitality, construction and the presidency's line of succession.

facts.t: Named for a Freedmen's Bureau chief.
facts.d: Gen. Oliver Otis Howard, commissioner of the Freedmen's Bureau, was a founder and served as university president from 1869 to 1874.
Howard is the only historically Black university classified as an R1 (very high research activity) doctoral university.
A 2018 Bloomberg Businessweek survey found 25 of 49 Howard School of Business graduates from 2010–2012 had started a company — the highest founder share among surveyed business schools.
Its radio station WHUR launched Cathy Hughes's broadcasting career; in 2016 the School of Communications was renamed for her after a multimillion-dollar gift from Alfred C. Liggins III.

name: University of the District of Columbia
affiliation: Public (District of Columbia); land-grant status under the 1966 D.C. School Reform Act; Thurgood Marshall College Fund member
formerNames: Normal School for Colored Girls (earliest predecessor)
Miner Normal School / Miner Teachers College (predecessor)
description: UDC is the only public university in Washington, D.C. It was formed on August 1, 1977, by consolidating Federal City College, Washington Technical Institute and District of Columbia Teachers College, and traces its founding to Myrtilla Miner's 1851 Normal School for Colored Girls. A commuter-heavy urban land-grant, it added the David A. Clarke School of Law in 1996 and a community college in 2009, and has long served working adults — including future media CEO Alfred C. Liggins III, who took night classes there.

facts.d: Its earliest predecessor, Myrtilla Miner's Normal School for Colored Girls, opened December 3, 1851 with six students — the first normal school in D.C.
Federal City College, Washington Technical Institute and D.C. Teachers College were consolidated on August 1, 1977, with Lisle C. Carter as first president.
The 1966 D.C. School Reform Act gave its predecessors land-grant status with a $7.24 million endowment in lieu of land.

name: Miner Teachers College
affiliation: Founded by abolitionist Myrtilla Miner with Quaker support; later part of the D.C. public school system
fate: In 1955, after Brown v. Board, it merged with the white Wilson Teachers College to form District of Columbia Teachers College.
description: Myrtilla Miner, a white abolitionist teacher from New York, opened the Normal School for Colored Girls in 1851 against mob hostility and official opposition, funded by Quakers and a $1,000 gift from Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin royalties. Reopened after the Civil War as Miner Normal School, it joined the D.C. public schools in 1879 and became the four-year Miner Teachers College in 1929, training generations of Black D.C. teachers. Its 1913 Georgia Avenue building is on the National Register of Historic Places.

facts.t: Fourth normal school in the U.S.
facts.d: It was the first normal school in D.C. and the fourth in the nation; enrollment grew from 6 to 40 within two months.
Benefactors included Quakers, Henry Ward Beecher and Harriet Beecher Stowe; Johns Hopkins sat on its 1856 board of trustees.
Congress made Miner Normal School a four-year teachers college in 1929.

name: Wayland Seminary
kind: Private HBCU · Baptist seminary and college
affiliation: American Baptist Home Mission Society (National Theological Institute)
fate: In 1899 it merged with Richmond Theological Seminary to form Virginia Union University in Richmond.
description: Wayland Seminary began in 1867 in the basement of Washington's First Colored Baptist Church (later Nineteenth Street Baptist) as the D.C. branch of the American Baptist Home Mission Society's National Theological Institute, named for anti-slavery Brown University president Francis Wayland. Led for 30 years by abolitionist George M. P. King, it offered ministerial, college, high-school and preparatory courses to freedmen and women. Its alumni include Booker T. Washington and Abyssinian Baptist pastor Adam Clayton Powell Sr.

name: Frelinghuysen University
kind: Private HBCU · Adult and evening university
affiliation: Independent; founded by Jesse and Rosetta Lawson
formerNames: Frelinghuysen Group of Schools for Colored Working People
fate: Lost accreditation in 1937 after Depression-era financial trouble, stopped awarding degrees, and had closed by 1964.
description: Founded in 1906 by activists Jesse and Rosetta Lawson, Frelinghuysen was the first school to offer evening and extension courses to Black working adults in Washington, holding classes in homes and businesses to cut commuting time and charging the lowest tuition possible. Scholar Anna J. Cooper served as president from 1930. It was accredited and awarded degrees from 1927 to 1937, and its John M. Langston School of Law fed faculty to the later Terrell Law School.

facts.d: Classes ran in local homes and businesses, with programs from basic literacy through undergraduate and graduate courses.
The renowned educator and author succeeded Jesse Lawson as president, taking office in 1930.
Frelinghuysen was accredited and awarded degrees from 1927 until 1937.

name: Robert H. Terrell Law School
affiliation: Independent; founded by George A. Parker and other Black D.C. lawyers
fate: Closed in 1950 after graduating about 600 lawyers, as other D.C. law schools integrated.
description: Founded in 1931 after Howard University ended its evening law program, Terrell Law School let working Black Washingtonians study law at night and, over 19 years, educated the majority of Black law students in the city. It was named for Robert Heberton Terrell, the long-serving Black judge of the D.C. Municipal Court. Alumni include D.C. Court of Appeals judge Austin L. Fickling, civil-rights leader Ruby Hurley and D.C. Council member Wilhelmina Rolark.

facts.d: Its founders created it when Howard closed its evening law school program.
The school graduated roughly 600 lawyers before closing in 1950.

name: Sean Combs

Forbes estimated he earned $130 million in the year to May 2017, ranking him first among entertainers.

legacyDetail.d: In June 2024 Howard's trustees unanimously revoked his honorary degree, ended a 2016 $1M gift agreement and disbanded the scholarship in his name.
